Data fields units acronyms and capture interpretation

Ubuntu VMware Telemetry Capture Guide

*A guide to the one minute passive sample*

This guide explains the Ubuntu environment record, collector settings, sample formats, field names, units, acronyms, and observed results from the 13 November 2026 VMware capture. The collector produced 61 host snapshots and 19,276 process rows in 60 seconds. The minute showed low guest-wide CPU use after the marked warm-up sample, stable available memory, and very small pressure-counter changes. It was a passive sample on Ubuntu 26.04.1, not an AIOS run, an Ubuntu 24.04 validation, or a controlled benchmark.

1 What was captured

The collector read host and process metrics through Python and psutil, plus Linux Pressure Stall Information (PSI) files under /proc/pressure. It wrote JSON Lines in the guest, and the output was copied into this project folder. The capture did not use sudo, eBPF, cgroup writes, process-priority changes, CPU affinity changes, or actuator actions.

The recorded window was 2026-11-13 18:23:31.050 UTC through 18:24:31.050 UTC. Each sampling pass records one host row and then one row for each visible process. The collector timestamps the pass once, so the host row and its process rows share the same UTC and monotonic timestamps. In this run, 316 process rows were written per pass: 61 x 316 = 19,276.

Collector parameters

OptionValue usedWhat it controls
--output/tmp/aios_telemetry_2026-11-13.jsonlGuest-side destination for the raw JSON Lines file. The retained copy is under this folder's recordings directory.
--interval1Requests a sampling cadence of one second. The recorded host timestamps are about one second apart.
--duration60Stops after about 60 elapsed seconds. The loop takes an immediate first sample and also samples at the 60-second boundary, giving 61 time points.
--host-aliasubuntu-26-04-vm01A label for this guest in the records; it is not the physical host name.
Privilege and controlsNo elevated accessThe command only reads telemetry and writes its output file. It does not change scheduling, memory limits, cgroups, or CPU placement.

Files and their roles

FileContentsHow to use it
telemetry.jsonl7,721,120 bytes; host and process records, one JSON object per line.Raw source of the time-series data. Keep local because PIDs, process start times, and resource readings can be sensitive.
host_samples.csv61 host-only rows and a flattened subset of host fields.Convenient for spreadsheet review. It omits process rows and some nested fields, so it is not a replacement for JSONL.
VM_Environment_Capture.txtA separate guest environment snapshot and collector checksum.Explains the OS, kernel, systemd, Python, psutil, CPU topology, memory, cgroup and PSI interfaces.
capture_manifest.jsonCapture provenance, counts, summary values, limitations, and hashes.Use to check where the sample came from and whether key files still match their recorded SHA-256 values.
VM_ReadOnly_Metadata_Capture.shThe read-only shell commands used to record guest metadata.Documents how the environment snapshot can be repeated.
README.mdShort capture interpretation and limitations.Quick orientation; this guide provides the longer explanation.

The JSONL file is the complete sample. The CSV is a convenience projection containing selected host fields only. For example, the raw host JSON retains per-CPU utilization, all three load averages, PSI some and full values, and disk operation counts; the CSV keeps a smaller set, including the one-minute load average, PSI some values, and disk byte totals.

Integrity values: telemetry.jsonl SHA-256 is 8cd652235a0d6429c9f41b2bb5c651339ddba5ef22f397d88c10a4df9529bdda. The collector source SHA-256 is b14379659d57b076945bbce18658f3db965ac95ec2ec5d4fbd6dc0030e1e35a7. The manifest contains hashes for the other captured files. SHA-256 fingerprints detect file changes; they do not encrypt the data.

2 Ubuntu environment explained

Ubuntu outputObserved valueMeaning and limit
DistributionUbuntu 26.04.1 LTS (Resolute)The guest operating system used for this capture. The project design target remains Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, so this is not target-version validation.
KernelLinux 7.0.0-43-generic, x86_64The guest's Linux kernel build and 64-bit x86 architecture.
systemd259.5-0ubuntu3.4The service and system manager version installed in the guest. This does not mean AIOS services were installed or running.
Python and psutilPython 3.14.4; psutil 7.1.0Runtime and library used by the read-only collector.
CPU topology2 logical CPUs; 1 thread per core; 1 core per socket; 2 sockets; 1 NUMA nodeThis is topology presented to the virtual machine. It does not reveal the physical host's core layout and does not show CPU pinning or a reserved AIOS core.
Memory3,513,298,944 bytes total; 44.9% used in the time seriesAbout 3.27 GiB (3.51 decimal GB) visible to the guest. Available memory stayed around 1.80 GiB (1.94 decimal GB).
Swap3,529,502,720 bytes total; 46,018,560 bytes usedAbout 3.29 GiB of swap, with about 43.9 MiB used (1.3%). This was essentially unchanged during the sample.
cgroup filesystemcgroup2fsThe guest exposed the unified cgroup v2 filesystem. Its presence alone does not prove that AIOS cgroups or resource limits were configured.
PSI interfacesCPU, memory and I/O readableThe collector could parse /proc/pressure/cpu, memory and io. A readable interface is not itself evidence of resource pressure.
Temporary filesystem/tmp mounted as tmpfs; 1% used in the metadata snapshotA temporary filesystem visible to the guest. It is not an AIOS persistence or storage benchmark.
Process inventory316 processes in the environment snapshotThe collector recorded 316 process rows at each time point. Names and command lines were intentionally omitted.

The environment text was captured at 18:27:17 UTC, after the telemetry window ended at 18:24:31 UTC. It is a separate point-in-time snapshot, so its memory readings can differ slightly from the time-series values without indicating an error.

3 How to read the records

Host record fields

FieldUnit or formMeaning and reading advice
record_typeTextIdentifies a row as host_sample or process_sample so readers can separate the two record types.
run_idUUID textOne generated identifier shared by all records in this collection run; use it to group the capture.
host_aliasTextThe label ubuntu-26-04-vm01 used for this guest.
boot_idUUID text; host rowsLinux boot identifier. It helps distinguish one boot session from another; it is not included in process rows.
ts_utcRFC 3339 timestampWall-clock time in UTC, shown with +00:00. Use it for human-readable ordering and cross-system comparison.
monotonic_nsNanosecondsMonotonic clock reading from the guest. Its absolute origin is not meaningful; subtract two readings to estimate elapsed time without wall-clock adjustments.
quality.cpu_first_interval_warmupTrue or FalseTrue on the first host CPU row. Exclude that row from CPU averages; it reads 66.7% and is explicitly marked as warm-up.
cpu_pctPercentGuest-wide CPU utilization across its two logical CPUs. This is total guest activity, including the collector and other guest processes; it is not the collector's CPU cost.
cpu_per_core_pctList of percentagesOne utilization value per guest logical CPU, in stable CPU order. These are guest-visible vCPUs, not verified physical cores.
load_averageThree numbersLinux load averages for 1, 5 and 15 minutes. They are queue/load indicators, not CPU percentages; they can include runnable and uninterruptible tasks. The capture started with history already accumulated before the one-minute run.
memory.total_bytesBytesPhysical memory visible to the guest, excluding swap.
memory.available_bytesBytesEstimate of memory that can be given to processes without forcing swap. Prefer this to the free-memory figure when judging headroom.
memory.used_bytes and memory.percentBytes and percentpsutil's informational used value and percentage. The percentage is calculated from total and available memory; cached memory means used and free do not simply add to total.
swap.total_bytes, used_bytes, free_bytes, percentBytes and percentGuest swap capacity and use. These fields are separate from physical RAM.
psi.<resource>.statusok / parse_error / unsupported_or_unreadableDescribes whether the collector could read and parse the PSI file. All captured CPU, memory and I/O status values were ok.
psi.<resource>.someavg10, avg60, avg300 percent; total microsecondsSome means at least one task was stalled on that resource. Averages describe the last 10, 60 and 300 seconds; total is cumulative since boot. Compare first and last totals for this run's change.
psi.<resource>.fullavg10, avg60, avg300 percent; total microsecondsFull means all non-idle tasks were stalled together. For system-wide CPU, the kernel defines full as unavailable and reports zero for compatibility, so CPU full=0 is not a CPU-pressure test result.
disk_io.read_bytes, write_bytesCumulative bytesGuest-visible aggregate disk counters. Subtract consecutive samples and divide by elapsed seconds for an approximate rate. They are not per-process or physical-host counters.
disk_io.read_count, write_countCumulative operationsGuest-visible aggregate operation counters. These are retained in JSONL but not in the host CSV.

Process record fields

FieldUnit or formMeaning and reading advice
process_ref.pidIntegerLinux process identifier. PIDs may be reused, so do not use the PID alone as a long-term identity.
process_ref.start_time_epoch_sUnix epoch secondsProcess start time. Paired with PID, it helps distinguish a new process from an older process that used the same PID.
statusTextProcess state at collection time, such as sleeping, idle or running. It is a point-in-time state, not a health rating.
cpu_pctPercent per processpsutil's process CPU use since its prior reading. It uses a different scale from host cpu_pct and can exceed 100% for multithreaded processes; do not sum process percentages as though they total 100%. Process rows have no separate warm-up flag.
rss_bytesBytesResident Set Size: non-swapped physical memory currently used by the process. Shared pages can appear in multiple processes, so summing RSS may double-count shared memory.
vms_bytesBytesVirtual Memory Size: the process's virtual address space. It is not the amount of physical RAM currently occupied.
io_counters.read_bytes / write_bytesCumulative bytes or nullPer-process byte counters when available. Null means unavailable in this row, not zero. This collector does not preserve a reason for every null.
quality.visibilityTextThe normal row says partial_if_permission_limited to warn that visibility may be incomplete. That label does not prove this row was denied. An explicit permission_denied row is a separate fallback emitted after AccessDenied.

If a process disappears or becomes inaccessible, the collector may skip a vanished process or emit a shorter permission-denied row with null values. A null, a numeric zero and an omitted field are different: null means unavailable, zero is an observed numeric value, and an omitted field may indicate that the fallback row could not supply it.

What the host CSV keeps

The CSV columns are ts_utc, monotonic_ns, cpu_pct, load_1m, memory_total_bytes, memory_used_bytes, memory_available_bytes, memory_pct, swap_used_bytes, CPU/memory/I/O PSI some averages and totals, disk read/write byte totals, and cpu_first_interval_warmup. It does not contain process-level rows, CPU-per-core values, the 5- and 15-minute load averages, PSI full values, or disk operation counts. Use telemetry.jsonl when those details matter.

4 What the sample shows

MeasureObserved resultPlain-language interpretation
Capture volume61 host samples; 19,276 process samples; 316 process rows per time point; one run IDThe collector continuously emitted both host and process records for the requested minute.
Host CPUFirst sample 66.7% and warm-up flagged. The remaining 60 samples averaged 1.392%, ranging from 0.5% to 2.0%.Guest-wide activity was low in this short sample after warm-up. This is not the collector's isolated CPU cost because no without-collector baseline was recorded.
RAMMemory stayed at 44.9% used. Available memory ranged from 1,935,966,208 to 1,936,355,328 bytes, about 1.80 GiB.The guest's available memory was stable during the minute. Linux's free-memory number was lower because available memory also accounts for reclaimable memory.
Swap46,018,560 bytes used (about 43.9 MiB, 1.3%); unchanged in the host CSV.No swap growth was observed in this short sample.
PSI averagesReported avg10 maximum was 0.00% for CPU, memory and I/O.No sustained recent pressure appeared at the precision of these rolling averages. A short average of zero does not mean no brief stall ever occurred.
PSI counter changesSome-stall total increased by 77,750 microseconds for CPU, 0 for memory and 5,898 microseconds for I/O. Full totals did not increase.These are small cumulative counter changes over the interval. Totals are since boot; differences are more useful than the absolute totals.
Guest disk countersRead-byte total did not change; write-byte total increased by 233,472 bytes.Only a small guest-visible write-counter change was recorded. This is not a disk performance or latency benchmark.
Process states13,786 sleeping; 5,426 idle; 64 running rows.Most process observations were sleeping or idle. These counts are rows across all time points, not unique processes per status.
Process I/O availability13,908 of 19,276 process rows had null I/O counters; 0 explicit permission_denied rows were recorded.The collector could not report I/O counters for many rows, and did not record why each counter was null. Do not treat null as zero or assume all nulls mean denied access.

Across all 61 host rows, available memory changed by 389,120 bytes (about 380 KiB). The first host row is included in this memory range; only its CPU value is marked as warm-up. This small range and the steady 44.9% memory value are descriptive of this VM during this one minute, not a guarantee under load.

What we can conclude

The collector ran successfully on this Ubuntu 26.04.1 VMware guest and wrote parseable host and process records.

The guest exposed cgroup v2 and readable CPU, memory and I/O PSI interfaces, which supports feasibility planning for those read-only inputs.

The observed minute had low guest-wide CPU use after the warm-up row, stable available memory, no swap increase, and zero PSI avg10 values at the recorded precision.

The capture includes no AI inference, prediction, decision, dashboard, actuator or resource-control execution. It cannot show that AIOS improves performance or is safe under control mode.

What we cannot conclude

Ubuntu 24.04 compatibility: the guest is Ubuntu 26.04.1 and runs a different kernel, systemd, Python and psutil build.

Collector overhead: host CPU includes the whole guest and the collector. No matched run with collection off was made, and the collector's own RAM/CPU was not isolated.

Behavior under workload: the minute was not a controlled load test and did not include labeled application behavior or a repeated baseline.

Core reservation or pinning: the 2-CPU topology is only what VMware presents to this guest. No CPU affinity or quota was applied or tested.

AIOS implementation or benefit: no AIOS services or model decisions were exercised, and no OS resource action occurred.

Recommended next evidence

Repeat the same read-only capture on the specified Ubuntu 24.04 target and retain its environment and checksum metadata.

To estimate collector cost, compare repeated matched runs with collection off and on, under both idle and approved representative workloads. Record collector-process CPU/RSS, host CPU/memory, PSI, and run-to-run variation.

Keep missing-data reasons explicit in future records, especially for per-process I/O counters, so unavailable, denied and unsupported values can be distinguished.

Keep resource-control experiments separate. Do not enable cgroup, priority or CPU-placement actions until bounds, ownership, rollback and safety checks have been reviewed and tested on the target host.

TermExpanded formMeaning here

GB / GiBGigabyte / GibibyteGB uses powers of 1,000; GiB uses powers of 1,024. The capture stores bytes; this guide labels both when useful.

6 Example records and how to read them

The first host row is timestamped 2026-11-13T18:23:31.050+00:00. It has record_type=host_sample, cpu_pct=66.7 and quality.cpu_first_interval_warmup=true. Keep the row as raw evidence, but exclude its CPU value from the steady-minute average. The same row reports 3,513,298,944 bytes total memory and 1,936,355,328 bytes available. Its CPU PSI some averages are avg10=0.00%, avg60=0.00% and avg300=0.06%; the longer windows include history from before this one-minute capture.

A process row from that same pass reports status=sleeping, cpu_pct=0.0, rss_bytes=17,571,840, vms_bytes=26,718,208 and io_counters=null. The process PID and start time are left out of this example, but they remain in the local raw JSONL. RSS is about 16.8 MiB and VMS about 25.5 MiB. The null I/O value means unavailable in that row; it is not a measured zero. Host and process rows share the timestamp because the collector creates one timestamp for each sampling pass.

08 Security safety and acceptance

Only admitted actions reach the actuator. Peer identity, message shape, action bounds, target identity, ownership, and result verification are checked before success can be reported. Recovery uses the same guarded path.

Guarded recovery

On unsafe or stale state, inhibit new AI writes. Restore a captured prior CPU weight only when the target is still valid and remains under AIOS control. Verify and audit the restoration. If safe restoration cannot be established, remain fail-closed and report degraded operation for host-side recovery.

Audit semantics

Decisions, denials, authentication and validation outcomes, action verification, and recovery outcomes belong in the audit design. A hash chain supports detection of alterations under the selected trust model; it does not make a compromised host incapable of rewriting local records. The storage, checkpoint, retention, failure, and privilege policies require an explicit implementation contract.

Complete safety acceptance cases

Test IDScenarioExpected safe resultStatus
ST-01Restart while default mode is OBSERVE_ONLYNo cgroup write; restart cannot enable control.Not run — prototype needed
ST-02Stale, missing, malformed or out-of-range sample/proposalLEAVE/deny with reason; no OS write; no silent zero-fill.Not run — thresholds/prototype needed
ST-03Unauthenticated Unix peer or malformed IPCSO_PEERCRED/payload validation rejects request; audit denial.Not run — UID policy/prototype needed
ST-04PID reused or process start time changesTarget identity mismatch rejects request.Not run — prototype needed
ST-05Target moved outside approved cgroupActuator rechecks allowlist/ownership and denies.Not run — allowlist/prototype needed
ST-06Dashboard POST/action/approval/mode/policy probeNo such route; dashboard has no actuator socket/write permission.Not run — deployable UI needed
ST-07Prior value changed by host owner before rollbackDo not overwrite unowned value; fail closed and audit.Not run — ownership policy needed
ST-08Watchdog heartbeat staleBlock new writes; safe restore only for verified AIOS-owned target.Not run — timing/prototype needed
ST-09Rollback target disappears or becomes uncertainNo guessed target; degraded fallback; audit outcome.Not run — prototype needed
ST-10SQLite/WAL cap or disk space reachedExpose degraded data state; stale/incomplete evidence cannot authorize control.Not run — retention policy needed
ST-11Audit chain altered, reordered, or truncatedIntegrity check detects break; automated writes disabled pending review.Not run — prototype/key policy needed
ST-12eBPF missing/denied; CPU mask unavailableExplicit unavailable/denied status; no escalation; stay observe-only.Not run — target host needed
ST-13Quota delays inference/watchdog or harms foregroundFail resource gate; retain OBSERVE_ONLY/revert profile.Not run — baseline/prototype needed
ST-14Service restart after degraded modeRestart preserves explicit safe mode; no hidden enablement.Not run — prototype needed

10 Resource budget and CPU placement

The optional selected-core approach concerns where AIOS compute services run and how much CPU time they may consume. Affinity, quota, weight, and physical-core isolation provide different controls.

Resource budget and placement analysis

AIOS Resource Budget and CPU Placement Recommendation

Host overhead, storage growth, and the optional fractional-core approach

Proposed design baseline. Not evidence of implementation or validation.

The CPU-core idea is an optional host-local experiment on selected compute units. Affinity chooses where they may run; CPUQuota caps CPU time and does not reserve guaranteed time. Watchdog, policy, and actuator stay outside an unvalidated tight quota. The project should establish whether AIOS improves a workload without becoming a new source of CPU contention, memory pressure, disk growth, or response delay.

1. Resource profile

ResourceAIOS useCost/failure modeInitial position
CPU timeSampling, validation, SQLite, generic inference, decisions, policy, actuator, dashboard queries, watchdog.Competes with user work; a tight quota can stale data or starve heartbeat.Measure total AIOS and selected compute slice separately; default unpinned, observe-only; keep watchdog/policy/actuator outside unvalidated tight quota.
CPU placementScheduler places selected AIOS compute units on allowed logical CPUs; workload control cgroups remain separate.Affinity is a placement restriction, not an exclusive core; SMT siblings share resources.Optional deployment experiment; CPU IDs come from host inventory.
MemoryPython services, in-memory sample window, SQLite cache, inference runtime/model.Large windows/model footprint can displace applications.Budget framework and model separately; model footprint is unknown pending colleague.
Persistent storageAccepted telemetry and bounded recommendation projection in SQLite; append-only hash-chain audit is separate logical storage; WAL.Raw per-process sampling can grow by GB/day; WAL adds temporary size.Bound retention and file size; do not persist raw high-frequency rows indefinitely.
Disk I/OBatched inserts, WAL/checkpoint, audit appends, dashboard reads.Frequent synchronous writes can worsen the I/O pressure being monitored.Measure bytes/s, transactions, checkpoint stalls and workload response.
Kernel interfacespsutil/procfs reads, fixed cgroup v2 CPU weight writes, optional eBPF.Permission errors, counter reset, kernel variation, unsafe target, probe overhead.Read-only first; eBPF off by default; fixed adapter only.
NetworkFastAPI status/recommendation/audit reads.Remote exposure can reveal process metadata or be mistaken for control.Local-only candidate default; remote viewing needs separate security review.
Energy/thermalOptional power/temperature readings for evaluation if hardware supports them.CPU profile may change energy/heat; interfaces differ.Measure only when reliable counters are available; no benefit claim.

3. Storage-growth calculation

Planning formula: daily process records = process count × 86,400 ÷ interval seconds. Estimated daily bytes = daily records × measured stored bytes per record. SQLite indexes, page slack, WAL, and metadata add to this estimate.

Illustrative assumptionEstimateConclusion
100 processes, 1-second sample, assumed 250 bytes/record8.64M rows/day; about 2.16 GB/day before indexes/WAL.Unbounded raw writes exceed a 512 MiB cap well before one day. Assumed row size is not measured.
Same process/sample size in a 5-minute memory ring100 × 300 × 250 B ≈ 7.5 MB payload estimate.Python object overhead can be much larger; measure RSS.
One-minute persisted summaries at same count/size100 × 1,440 × 250 B ≈ 36 MB/day before indexes/WAL.Candidate compact-retention path; benchmark actual bytes and write cost.

Recommended path: keep a short inference window in a bounded memory ring; use SQLite for accepted telemetry and a compact read-only recommendation projection; keep the append-only hash-chain audit as separate logical storage with its own integrity/retention policy. Raw traces use a separate quota and privacy-reviewed export.

4. CPU placement alternatives

ProfileMechanismBenefit to testRisk / correct interpretationRecommendation
A. BaselineNo pinning or quota.Reference condition and simplest profile.AIOS may migrate and contend across allowed CPUs.Required safe default.
B. AffinityCPUAffinity= per selected compute service or AllowedCPUs= on an AIOS compute slice.Restricts AIOS to chosen logical CPU(s).Other tasks/kernel activity may share; parent cgroups can narrow effective set.Benchmark after baseline; no exclusivity claim.
C. Fractional shareAffinity plus CPUQuota=; systemd maps quota to cgroup v2 cpu.max. Example 20% caps at 20% of one CPU.Limits selected compute-slice CPU time to a chosen ceiling.Ceiling is not reservation/minimum. Low cap may delay inference or sampling; watchdog, policy, and actuator stay outside until worst-case delay is measured. CPUWeight is relative share, not a cap.Best match to ‘part of a core’; experiment after protecting safety path.
D. Isolated physical coreIsolated cpuset/boot config, IRQ routing and SMT handling.May reduce selected types of scheduler/kernel interference.Host-wide, invasive, reduces capacity; SMT/IRQ/kernel noise matter; housekeeping CPU required.Later research only; not default or first prototype.

Figure 1. Editable Mermaid CPU placement profile in 01_Diagrams.

5. Profile selection and safeguards

Record online logical CPU IDs, physical-core and SMT topology. Never hard-code CPU 0 or treat one logical CPU as a physical core.

Check effective CPU masks after parent cgroup constraints; if requested CPU is unavailable, remove affinity or enter OBSERVE_ONLY and report it.

Keep AIOS service placement cgroups separate from monitored workload cgroups.

Do not put watchdog or actuator heartbeat under an experimental low quota until worst-case heartbeat and rollback delay pass measurement.

Compare A then B, then C with team-selected candidate quotas. D requires host-owner approval and rollback procedure.

CPUQuota is a maximum CPU-time allowance, not reserved execution time. CPUWeight only changes relative distribution under contention.

6. Evaluation matrix

ScenarioRecordDecision question
Idle/interactive baselineAIOS CPU/RSS, wakeups, freshness, foreground p50/p95.Does collection alone create measurable overhead?
CPU-bound foreground + backgroundPer-core/cgroup CPU, throughput/latency, inference and heartbeat age.Does placement/quota cause contention or starvation?
Memory pressurePSI, RSS, swap, faults, sample quality.Does the agent’s own footprint worsen memory pressure?
I/O pressurePSI, DB/WAL bytes, write rate, insert/checkpoint latency, workload I/O.Does telemetry worsen the pressure it observes?
Process churn / PID reuseIdentity continuity, stale samples, target/cgroup identity.Can proposals stay attached to the correct process instance?
Failure injectionNo PSI, eBPF error, stale heartbeat, wrong peer, malformed request, disk full, actuator failure.Does it fail closed, continue Linux native behavior and audit outcome?
A/B/C CPU comparisonSame host/workloads, effective mask, CPU time, freshness, app p95/throughput.Does placement help enough to justify complexity and capacity loss?

Proposed practice: record host/kernel/systemd versions and workload; hold configuration constant; warm up consistently; repeat each condition at least 10 times if feasible; report medians, p95, spread, and failed runs. This repetition count is a planning suggestion. If safety or budget evidence is inconclusive, retain OBSERVE_ONLY.

7. Recommendation

Keep default scheduling and OBSERVE_ONLY as baseline. Evaluate affinity first. To express a fraction of one logical CPU, pair host-selected AllowedCPUs/CPUAffinity with a quota cap, and describe it as an upper bound. Avoid isolated physical-core work until a measured need and operations review exist. Apply optional quota only to a reviewed compute slice separate from watchdog/policy/actuator; measure host interference before enabling runtime action.

CPU affinity design note

Optional AIOS CPU Placement and Fractional-Core Profile

Recommendation

Keep ordinary scheduling and OBSERVE_ONLY as the baseline. Treat placement as an optional host-local experiment. If the team wants to allocate only a fraction of one CPU to AIOS, combine affinity to a host-selected logical CPU set with systemd CPUQuota= / cgroup-v2 cpu.max. A quota is a maximum CPU-time allowance, not a guaranteed reservation. Do not isolate a physical core in the first prototype.

Four profiles

1. Baseline: no pinning or quota; required comparison.

2. Affinity: CPUAffinity= per service or AllowedCPUs= on an AIOS slice. It restricts where AIOS can run; other tasks and kernel work may still share the CPU. Verify effective CPUs because parent cgroups can narrow the set.

3. Affinity plus fractional quota: a selected CPU set plus CPUQuota=. CPUQuota=20% is an illustrative upper cap of 20% of one CPU's time, not a chosen implementation or a reservation. A low cap may delay inference, sampling, heartbeat, and rollback. CPUWeight= is relative sharing, not a cap.

4. Isolated physical core: isolated cpuset/boot configuration, IRQ and housekeeping considerations. This is host-wide and invasive. SMT siblings, IRQs, kernel work and firmware noise affect isolation; Linux requires a housekeeping CPU. Defer unless measured need and host-level review justify it.

Evaluation

Compare profiles A/B/C on one recorded Ubuntu host. Measure AIOS per-service/total CPU, p95 sample-to-decision age, heartbeat delay, RSS, foreground p95 latency/throughput, disk growth and effective CPU mask. Include CPU, memory, I/O, mixed load, missing/stale data and watchdog faults. Keep OBSERVE_ONLY if safety invariants or agreed budgets fail. Profile D needs separate operations/security approval and rollback instructions.

References

[Linux CPU isolation](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/admin-guide/cpu-isolation.html)

[Linux housekeeping](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/core-api/housekeeping.html)

A blocked or unsupported gate keeps the affected resource in recommendation-only mode.

5. Whole-project effort estimate

The estimate is a bottom-up, range-based planning estimate from the work packages, team task dependencies, end-to-end product boundary, safety gates and required evidence. A person-day is eight focused hours of project work and includes engineering, integration, testing, review and evidence work; idle waiting for access or course decisions is a schedule risk, not productive effort. The range is a low-confidence planning judgment, not a PERT calculation, statistical confidence interval, contractual quote, measured velocity or remaining-work estimate. A previously stated 15% uplift had no project-specific evidence and is withdrawn; no contingency is included. Before baselining a reserve, the Developers must review work-package uncertainty and quantified risk exposure.

How Scrum estimation will work

The Scrum Guide assigns Product Backlog item sizing to the Developers and says the Sprint forecast should use past performance, upcoming capacity and the Definition of Done. It does not prescribe story points, a point scale, or a conversion from points to days. [1]

During ongoing refinement, the Developers split each outcome into a testable Product Backlog item with a clear acceptance check, dependency, risk, owner for coordination and evidence location.

Use relative size as a team tactic: planning poker with Fibonacci values 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 and 13. Items larger than 8–13 points should usually be split or clarified; the threshold is a local rule, not a Scrum requirement.

Do not convert story points to person-days. Keep the person-day range for whole-project effort/capacity planning and relative points for team Sprint forecasting.

The Notion snapshot has no completed-point history or measured velocity. At the first planning session, inspect real item status and confirm member availability. After two consecutive Sprints with verified Done items and known capacity, use the team’s observed throughput to forecast; never invent velocity or count unfinished work as Done.

At each Sprint Planning, select work by the Developers’ actual availability after exams, holidays, review duties and dependencies; create one Sprint Goal and a visible Sprint Backlog. Reforecast when scope, evidence, risk or capacity changes.

Capacity and schedule sensitivity

Capacity uses the five contributor labels in the retained task baseline, assuming each can provide 2.5–3.5 focused project days in a two-week Sprint after classes, exams and other commitments. Count planning/review/retrospective time inside project capacity when selecting backlog items. Confirm actual availability; official course guidance allows five to six students, but no capacity is credited to an unconfirmed sixth member.

ScenarioCapacity per Sprint16-Sprint capacityPlanning implication
Low availability12.5 person-days200 person-daysThe 195-day upper base estimate leaves only 5 days of headroom; approved contingency or rework may require more Sprints or an explicit scope decision.
Working baseline15 person-days240 person-daysThe 195-day upper base estimate leaves 45 days before any contingency; confirm availability and reforecast with actual evidence.
High availability17.5 person-days280 person-daysCovers the current base range with 85 days before any contingency, subject to exams, holidays, task dependencies and technical gates.

These are aggregate forecast cases, not commitments. Because Sprints 1–3 have passed on the proposed calendar and the task board has no effort history, the team must verify accepted work and remaining items before presenting a remaining-effort number. If remaining effort exceeds capacity to the course date, preserve safety/evaluation work and either extend the forecast or obtain an explicit scope decision.

7. Scrum operating model

Use Scrum as the complete empirical framework, not a status-meeting label. The Scrum Guide defines accountabilities, events, artifacts and commitments, while leaving estimation units and many team tactics to the team. This plan adopts two-week Sprints and a collaborative relative-sizing technique; the team must retain the Product Goal, Sprint Goal, Definition of Done, inspection, and adaptation. [1]

ElementAIOS implementation
Product GoalA bounded single-host system that monitors and processes resource evidence, predicts risk, makes a separately policy-admitted decision, safely actuates only approved cgroups when authorized, verifies/audits the change, and reports evidence.
Product BacklogUse the shared Notion task list as the seed. Product Owner keeps one ordered source of work; refinement adds outcome, acceptance evidence, dependencies, risk, size and traceability. Keep course/research deliverables visible.
Sprint PlanningWhole Scrum Team agrees why the Sprint is valuable and a single Sprint Goal; Developers select work based on actual capacity and prepare an actionable plan. Proposed timebox: up to 2 hours for a two-week Sprint.
Daily Scrum15-minute event for Developers on each working day, focused on Sprint Goal progress and the next actionable plan. If the team uses an asynchronous status note, treat it as coordination and still arrange the formal event or explicitly document a Scrum adaptation.
Backlog refinementOngoing, usually one short weekly working session. Split items, clarify acceptance criteria/dependencies and size work; it is not a formal Scrum event.
Sprint ReviewWorking review of the increment with the supervisor/stakeholders when available; inspect results and adapt backlog, not only a slide presentation. Proposed timebox: 60–90 minutes.
Sprint RetrospectiveInspect collaboration, quality, tools and Definition of Done; select one improvement with owner and next review. Proposed timebox: 60 minutes.
Sprint BacklogSprint Goal + selected Product Backlog items + a plan created and updated by Developers. Track impediments and evidence links in the shared task board.
Increment / Definition of DoneOnly reviewed, verified work that meets the project Definition of Done counts as an increment. Designs, open tasks and untested code do not establish integrated product behavior.

Definition of Ready for Sprint selection

One clear outcome tied to Product Goal or course/research obligation; small enough to finish within a Sprint, or explicitly split.

Acceptance check, test/evidence artifact, dependency, data/privacy boundary and accountable coordination owner are visible.

Relative size is agreed by Developers; unresolved design choices are recorded as spikes with a question and decision output.

Any privileged-action item identifies the resource owner, target capability, authorization, bounds, rollback, failure behavior and gate; otherwise it is not ready for an enabled write.

Definition of Done for an AIOS increment

Acceptance criteria and relevant unit, integration, data-quality, security, failure or evaluation checks pass; failed checks are visible and linked.

A peer reviews the change; interface, requirement traceability, diagrams and source/render pairs are updated where affected.

Evidence is reproducible and scoped; statuses distinguish proposed, implemented, verified and measured. No claim is stronger than its evidence.

Data handling, storage caps, permissions and audit impact are reviewed. For an action, independent authorization, allow-list, bounds, read-back, audit and recovery checks pass.

The increment integrates with prior increments and can be demonstrated safely. An unsafe or unsupported action remains disabled and returns a recommendation.

11. Change control and project decisions

Any change to resource controls, user interaction, data fields, deployment privileges, project type, research question or target host is a Product Backlog decision and is logged with rationale, owner, date, impact and evidence.

A scope change that affects safety, cost, course milestones or estimates must update the SRS, diagrams, interfaces, risk register, test/evaluation plan and release package before it is treated as accepted scope.

The Product Owner orders the backlog; Developers decide implementation approach and Sprint forecast. Team-wide or supervisor decisions are recorded where the course requires them. Only Product Owner can cancel a Sprint when its Goal is obsolete. [1]

Changes do not reduce the Definition of Done or remove safety, evaluation, privacy and evidence controls to create apparent schedule progress.

12. Completion and handoff criteria

The team and supervisor have recorded Product Goal, Research/Product project type, roster, Scrum accountability assignments, target host, workload, data boundary and final course dates.

The full monitor → process → predict → policy → bounded action path has a repeatable test trace; any resource that did not pass its gate is clearly marked advisory/disabled, with no unsupported live-write claim.

Every Must requirement has an acceptance result or documented exception; performance claims link to target-host run IDs, metrics, baseline, configuration and limitations.

All action paths enforce authorization, approved cgroup/process identity, resource-specific bounds, cooldown, read-back, audit and tested recovery; unsafe/stale/unsupported cases do not write.

The final research paper/report, release notes, diagrams, test/evaluation evidence, risks, package manifest and presentation are peer-reviewed and handed off with open work named.

12 Research framing and evaluation

The research framing compares proposed forecasting and bounded control with available Linux mechanisms. Evaluation must measure workload benefit as well as AIOS overhead and safety.

Research paper draft

Design and Evaluation of a Policy-Gated Linux Resource Management Agent

First-semester Research Paper draft · track confirmed

Proposed design baseline. Not evidence of implementation or validation.

This draft includes motivation/problem, objectives, literature survey, solution approaches, methodology, and an initial implementation plan. It contains no experimental result, survey finding, model-type claim, or submission claim. AI model internals remain with the colleague assigned to them.

Abstract

Linux exposes resource observations such as utilization, process counters, cgroup controls, and Pressure Stall Information (PSI). Existing mechanisms can report current pressure or apply configured responses, while an AIOS prediction layer adds computation, storage, security, and mis-action risks. This paper proposes the design and evaluation of AIOS, a user-space resource-management agent for Ubuntu 24.04. A Python collector validates host/process telemetry; generic inference services return per-process outputs; decision and policy services produce LEAVE or a bounded proposal; Unix-socket peer authentication, actuator revalidation, append-only audit, and watchdog fallback constrain control. OBSERVE_ONLY is the default. The product target includes separately gated bounded CPU, RAM, and supported I/O controls on preconfigured groups, with CPU first in the implementation phase. Evaluation will compare AIOS against PSI/systemd baselines under controlled CPU, memory, I/O, and mixed workloads. This draft defines metrics and a CPU-placement experiment. No improvement is claimed before data collection.

Keywords: Linux resource management; PSI; cgroups v2; policy-gated control; CPU affinity; CPU quota; system observability.

1. Introduction and problem definition

A resource-intensive foreground process may become unresponsive even when a single utilization number does not reveal whether tasks are stalled on CPU, memory, or I/O. Linux PSI exposes current pressure signals. Linux cgroups v2 and systemd provide resource-control interfaces. These mechanisms make an adaptive resource prototype plausible but do not prove that a prediction layer will help on Ubuntu hardware.

Problem statement: a model-guided control agent may add useful early per-process recommendations, but it also consumes the same CPU, memory, storage, and I/O resources it observes and can apply a wrong action. The research question is whether a model-independent, policy-gated architecture can deliver measurable value without unacceptable overhead or unsafe host changes. The project treats this as a hypothesis to test, not a demonstrated deficiency in Linux.

2. Objectives and research questions

Objective / research questionEvidence needed
O1. Specify a model-independent telemetry → inference → decision → policy → actuator architecture.Reviewed SRS, diagrams, security and interface decisions.
O2. Compare PSI/current-threshold response with future-onset per-process recommendations.Named baselines and controlled test traces.
O3. Measure AIOS CPU, memory, disk, latency, freshness and workload interference.Target-host baseline and enabled runs.
O4. Verify denial/fallback for stale data, PID reuse, untrusted IPC, invalid bounds and watchdog failure.Negative/failure tests and audit evidence.
O5. Evaluate placement on one logical CPU and a fractional CPU-time cap.A/B/C profiles, topology, application p95 and watchdog freshness.
RQ1. How much earlier, if at all, can generic outputs identify pressure onset than a PSI threshold?Event labels, prediction horizon, false alarms and held-out evaluation from AI owner.
RQ2. Does bounded CPU weight improve a selected workload metric over observe-only within the resource budget?Matched workload runs and preselected success metric.
RQ3. How do affinity and quota affect AIOS timeliness and host workload performance?Per-profile measurements on same host.
RQ4. Do the security/safety controls reject unsafe requests under defined faults?Zero accepted out-of-policy writes in negative tests is a target, not a result.

3. Background and literature review

PSI reports time in which some or all non-idle tasks stall on CPU, memory, or I/O; it is observed pressure, not a future forecast (Linux Kernel Documentation, 2024). systemd-oomd uses PSI and cgroups v2 to poll configured units and may terminate eligible cgroups when configured thresholds are exceeded (systemd, 2024). These are important reactive baselines; AIOS must demonstrate incremental value beyond current pressure and configured response.

Alicherry and Gopinath (2001) studied resource containers and Linux CPU scheduling to account for activity-level resource use. Redline coordinated CPU scheduling with memory and disk I/O management to protect interactive application responsiveness. These works establish that containerized attribution and multi-resource coordination are existing research directions; AIOS should not claim those ideas as novel. Caladan (Fried et al., 2020) studied rapid core allocation under changing interference and cautions against assuming static core partitioning is always sufficient. Its dedicated scheduler/kernel module targets specialized workloads and is not treated as a drop-in solution.

SourceContribution used hereLimit for AIOS comparison
Linux PSI + cgroup v2 docsCurrent pressure accounting and Linux CPU-control interfaces.No forecast or guaranteed placement claim.
systemd-oomd docsConfigured pressure monitoring and cgroup termination response.Different intervention semantics from AIOS’s bounded and independently gated CPU/RAM/I/O product target.
Alicherry & Gopinath (2001)Activity/resource containers and CPU scheduling in Linux.Older kernel implementation; historical context.
Redline (Yang et al., 2008)Integrated CPU/memory/I/O management and responsiveness evaluation.Kernel extension with broader controls.
Caladan (Fried et al., 2020)Core allocation under interference and performance trade-offs.Specialized scheduler and kernel module; different workload scale.

4. Literature search approach and solution options

A targeted scoping search was performed 13 November 2026 using official Linux Kernel documentation, systemd v255 manuals, Ubuntu Noble package records, and primary USENIX/OSDI papers. Queries covered PSI/resource pressure; cgroup v2 CPU weight, quota and cpuset; systemd 255 controls and systemd-oomd; Linux CPU isolation/housekeeping; resource containers; Redline; and Caladan. Include official or primary sources relevant to measurement, controls, baseline behavior, or placement cost. Exclude marketing claims, unsupported cross-workload performance claims, and model-specific work outside Ammar’s scope. This is not a systematic review; exhaustive database coverage and screening counts are not claimed. See 10_Evidence_Closure/Research_Source_Log.csv for query and claim-level limits.

ApproachStrengthRisk/gapRole in study
Read-only monitorLow control risk; overhead baseline.No autonomous recommendation.Required baseline.
Current threshold responseInterpretable; similar to configured PSI/systemd action.Reactive and dependent on threshold choice.Comparison baseline.
Prediction → policy → bounded CPU weightTests early per-process recommendation and narrow reversible control.Model error, process identity, and overhead need strict safeguards.Proposed research path; observe-only first.
Broad CPU/memory/I/O autonomous controlCould affect multiple resource bottlenecks.Different and potentially destructive semantics; larger blast radius.Unbounded control is excluded. Bounded RAM and supported I/O actions require separate gates and follow the CPU-first phase.
AIOS CPU affinity/fractional quotaMay constrain placement and bound agent CPU consumption.Affinity is not exclusivity; quota is a cap, not reservation.Optional experiment after baseline.

5. Proposed methodology and system design

Figure 1. Proposed model-independent architecture. Editable source is in 01_Diagrams.

The collector reads available host and process counters, validates time, units, quality and process identity, then stores bounded local data. Generic inference outputs feed a decision builder that produces LEAVE or a proposal per eligible process. The policy gate checks mode, target, allowlist, freshness, bounds, and cooldown. For an admitted resource action, a local Unix socket authenticates the peer through SO_PEERCRED; the actuator repeats identity, target, ownership, range, and matching capability checks, then uses a fixed resource adapter. The system verifies and records the result in a hash-chained log. A watchdog blocks new writes and attempts rollback only for a verified AIOS-owned target. The user dashboard is query-only.

StageInitial implementation planStatus
Observe/validatePython psutil + procfs PSI; optional fixed eBPF adapter; mark missing data explicitly.Proposed; cadence/fields pending.
PersistSQLite, bounded retention; in-memory rolling window for inference.Proposed; candidate schema in 14_Data_Model; approval pending.
AssessGeneric inference outputs; per-process decision and LEAVE.Model types and internals excluded.
Gate/actuateOBSERVE_ONLY first; optional CPU weight only on allowlisted groups; secure local IPC and revalidation.Proposed; security review pending.
Audit/fallback/viewHash-chained append; watchdog; read-only FastAPI projection.Proposed; implementation not evidenced.

6. Evaluation design

Use a comparative experiment on a recorded Ubuntu 24.04 host. Record host CPU topology/SMT, RAM, storage, kernel/systemd versions, cgroup mode, background services and workload configuration. Compare AIOS absent, AIOS OBSERVE_ONLY, and only later any reviewed bounded CPU-control profile. Hold software/configuration constant within comparisons, warm up consistently, repeat runs where feasible, and report distributions and failures.

DimensionCandidate metricInterpretation
PredictionLead time before agreed PSI event; event-level false alarms and missed events using labels/horizon set by model owner.Compare against PSI threshold; exact model metric contract TBD.
Workload outcomeLatency, throughput, or completion time selected for each workload.Baseline vs observe-only vs bounded CPU weight.
Agent overheadCPU time, RSS, database/WAL bytes, write rate.AIOS absent vs enabled; model runtime reported separately.
TimelinessSample age, inference/decision time, actuator verification, heartbeat delay.Assess 1s-cadence candidate and CPU profiles.
SafetyOut-of-policy writes, wrong-target writes, unauthorized peers, fallback outcome.Target is zero accepted violations in negative tests, not a measured claim.
Data qualityCoverage, missing-source/reset rate, time alignment, process identity continuity.Disclose exclusions; no silent imputation.

Candidate workload set: idle/interactive, CPU-bound, memory pressure, I/O pressure, mixed pressure, process churn, missing PSI, stale telemetry, IPC rejection, disk-full and watchdog failure. Sampling period, prediction horizon, labels, statistical tests and final budgets must be approved before results are collected.

7. Dataset plan, ethics, and limitations

Primary data should come from controlled workloads on the intended Ubuntu host because that can pair PSI, process identity, cgroup context and application outcome. Public cluster traces such as Alibaba’s provide workload/resource context but are not assumed to include the same PSI and desktop process fields required for direct evaluation. Synthetic stress tests can verify the pipeline but do not replace realistic host data. No dataset has been selected or collected in this package.

Minimize data: use opaque host aliases and PID plus start time; omit command line, username, environment, paths and payload data by default. Obtain host/participant approval before recording. A hash chain provides tamper evidence for linked records but does not by itself guarantee tamper-proof storage.

8. Expected contribution and next steps

Expected contribution is an evaluated model-independent integration and safety design, with evidence about forecast value, bounded-action safety, overhead and CPU-placement trade-offs. This is proposed work, not a novelty claim or result. Prior work already covers pressure monitoring, resource containers, cross-resource scheduling and dynamic core allocation.

Complete literature search log and inclusion criteria with supervisor review.

Agree team project type, stakeholders, host, interface, sampling cadence, policy bounds, retention and resource gates.

Collect local market/user evidence if required; no survey findings are asserted here.

Record read-only Ubuntu baseline and test storage, CPU, memory and foreground impact.

Implement observe-only before any actuation; treat model runtime and model performance as colleague-owned dependencies.

Complete GP2 implementation, evaluation, results and final research-paper submission preparation.

13 Recorded evidence and interpretation

The retained passive run contains 61 host samples and 19,276 process rows. Its format, CSV projection, and five listed file hashes passed the package validator. It was collected on Ubuntu 26.04.1; the design target is Ubuntu 24.04.

Ubuntu commands and results

Ubuntu Command Evidence and Results

Plain-language guide to the archived VM commands, parameters, outputs and sample limits

Provenance The PNGs are rendered cards from the archived script and saved output, not original VMware terminal screenshots. The console image was unavailable. Saved script, output text and raw telemetry are the evidence.

1 What was recorded

A Python/psutil collector read guest and process metrics and Linux PSI counters for one minute. The manifest records a requested 1-second interval, 60-second duration and run ID a5f4346b-080c-40e2-a17e-4140d0ce7c53. Each pass emits one host row and one row per visible process.

The guest was Ubuntu 26.04.1 LTS in VMware, not Ubuntu 24.04. No AIOS daemon, model, policy action or resource control ran. Collection did not change scheduling or cgroups; it wrote its output file under /tmp.

2 Command evidence cards

Cards cover all 15 metadata commands preserved in VM_ReadOnly_Metadata_Capture.sh and the collector invocation from the manifest. Collector counts were independently derived from JSONL because original terminal stdout was not saved.

4 Sampling and data interpretation

Why 61 samples

The collector emits an immediate first sample and another at the 60-second boundary. Thus a 60-second period at one-second cadence contains 61 host timestamps. Each has 316 process rows, giving 316 × 61 = 19,276 observations. These are repeated process observations, not unique processes.

The first psutil CPU interval is marked warm-up; its 66.7% value is not steady-state evidence. The manifest reports mean CPU 1.392%, min 0.5%, max 2.0% after warm-up. This describes one passive minute, not a benchmark or representative baseline.

PSI terms

PSI is Pressure Stall Information. “some” counts time when at least some non-idle tasks stall; “full” counts time when all non-idle tasks stall together where available. avg10/avg60/avg300 are rolling stall percentages over about 10/60/300 seconds. total is cumulative microseconds since boot. These are counters and rolling averages, not predictions or diagnoses.

Bytes, CSV and CPU placement

JSONL is the source of truth. The 24-column CSV is a convenience projection. The previous CSV rounded monotonic_ns to scientific notation and had a stale manifest size/hash. It was regenerated from unchanged JSONL with exact integer timestamps; the validator checks every projected field and all listed hashes.

cgroup2fs only confirms the v2 mount was visible; no cgroup was written. Affinity limits eligible logical CPUs. CPUQuota caps CPU time. Neither reserves a physical core; isolated-core placement is a separate host/kernel/topology experiment.

14 Collector and reproducibility materials

The collector is the retained read-only acquisition artifact. The design diagrams do not establish that the inference, policy, actuator, watchdog, or dashboard services have been integrated.

Full read-only collector source
#!/usr/bin/env python3

"""Linux-only, read-only AIOS host/process recorder. Emits JSON Lines."""

import argparse,datetime,json,os,platform,time,uuid

from pathlib import Path

try: import psutil

except ImportError: raise SystemExit("Install psutil: python3 -m pip install psutil")

def text(path):

 try:return Path(path).read_text(encoding="utf-8",errors="replace")

 except OSError:return None

def psi(resource):

 raw=text(f"/proc/pressure/{resource}")

 if raw is None:return {"status":"unsupported_or_unreadable","some":None,"full":None}

 try:

  result={}

  for line in raw.splitlines():

   bits=line.split();vals={}

   for pair in bits[1:]:

    k,v=pair.split("=",1);vals[k]=float(v) if k.startswith("avg") else int(v)

   result[bits[0]]=vals

  return {"status":"ok","some":result.get("some"),"full":result.get("full")}

 except (ValueError,IndexError):return {"status":"parse_error","some":None,"full":None}

def safe(fn):

 try:return fn()

 except (OSError,psutil.Error,AttributeError):return None

def main():

 ap=argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__);ap.add_argument("--output",required=True)

 ap.add_argument("--interval",type=float,default=1);ap.add_argument("--duration",type=float,default=0);ap.add_argument("--host-alias",default="host-local");a=ap.parse_args()

 if platform.system()!="Linux":raise SystemExit("Linux required; no telemetry collected on this host.")

 if not 0<a.interval<=60:raise SystemExit("interval must be >0 and <=60 seconds")

 dest=Path(a.output).expanduser();dest.parent.mkdir(parents=True,exist_ok=True);fd=os.open(str(dest),os.O_CREAT|os.O_APPEND|os.O_WRONLY,0o600)

 run=str(uuid.uuid4());psutil.cpu_percent(None)

 for p in psutil.process_iter():

  try:p.cpu_percent(None)

  except psutil.Error:pass

 start=time.monotonic();deadline=start;cycle=0

 try:

  with os.fdopen(fd,"a",encoding="utf-8",buffering=1) as out:

   while True:

    now=datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc).isoformat(timespec="milliseconds");mono=time.monotonic_ns()

    vm=safe(psutil.virtual_memory);sw=safe(psutil.swap_memory);disk=safe(psutil.disk_io_counters)

    host={"record_type":"host_sample","run_id":run,"host_alias":a.host_alias,"boot_id":(text("/proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id") or "").strip() or None,

     "ts_utc":now,"monotonic_ns":mono,"quality":{"cpu_first_interval_warmup":cycle==0},

    "cpu_pct":safe(lambda:psutil.cpu_percent(None)),"cpu_per_core_pct":safe(lambda:psutil.cpu_percent(percpu=True)),"load_average":safe(os.getloadavg),

     "memory":({"total_bytes":vm.total,"available_bytes":vm.available,"used_bytes":vm.used,"percent":vm.percent} if vm else None),

     "swap":({"total_bytes":sw.total,"used_bytes":sw.used,"free_bytes":sw.free,"percent":sw.percent} if sw else None),

     "psi":{r:psi(r) for r in ("cpu","memory","io")},

     "disk_io":({"read_bytes":disk.read_bytes,"write_bytes":disk.write_bytes,"read_count":disk.read_count,"write_count":disk.write_count} if disk else None)}

    out.write(json.dumps(host,separators=(",",":"))+"\n")

    for p in psutil.process_iter():

     try:

      with p.oneshot():

       mi=p.memory_info();io=safe(p.io_counters)

       row={"record_type":"process_sample","run_id":run,"host_alias":a.host_alias,"ts_utc":now,"monotonic_ns":mono,

        "process_ref":{"pid":p.pid,"start_time_epoch_s":p.create_time()},"status":p.status(),

        "cpu_pct":p.cpu_percent(None),"rss_bytes":mi.rss,"vms_bytes":mi.vms,

        "io_counters":({"read_bytes":io.read_bytes,"write_bytes":io.write_bytes} if io else None),

        "quality":{"visibility":"partial_if_permission_limited"}}

      out.write(json.dumps(row,separators=(",",":"))+"\n")

     except (psutil.NoSuchProcess,psutil.ZombieProcess):continue

     except psutil.AccessDenied:

      out.write(json.dumps({"record_type":"process_sample","run_id":run,"host_alias":a.host_alias,"ts_utc":now,

       "monotonic_ns":mono,"process_ref":{"pid":p.pid,"start_time_epoch_s":None},"cpu_pct":None,"rss_bytes":None,

       "quality":{"visibility":"permission_denied"}},separators=(",",":"))+"\n")

    cycle+=1

    if a.duration and time.monotonic()-start>=a.duration:break

    deadline+=a.interval;time.sleep(max(0,deadline-time.monotonic()))

 except KeyboardInterrupt:pass

if __name__=="__main__":main()

  printf '\n[cpu_topology]\n'; lscpu | grep -E '^(Architecture|CPU\(s\)|Thread\(s\) per core|Core\(s\) per socket|Socket\(s\)|NUMA node\(s\)):'
  printf '\n[memory]\n'; free -b
  printf '\n[filesystem_tmp]\n'; df -P /tmp
  printf '\n[process_count]\n'; ps -e --no-headers | wc -l
  printf '\n[cgroup_filesystem]\n'; stat -fc '%T' /sys/fs/cgroup
  printf '\n[psi_cpu]\n'; cat /proc/pressure/cpu 2>&1 || true
  printf '\n[psi_memory]\n'; cat /proc/pressure/memory 2>&1 || true
  printf '\n[psi_io]\n'; cat /proc/pressure/io 2>&1 || true
  printf '\n[collector_sha256]\n'; sha256sum /tmp/aios_readonly_collector.py
} > "$OUT"
printf '%s\n' "$OUT"
Capture validation source
#!/usr/bin/env python3

"""Verify a retained AIOS telemetry capture without modifying its raw JSONL."""

import argparse,csv,hashlib,json

from collections import Counter

from pathlib import Path

FIELDS = ['ts_utc', 'monotonic_ns', 'cpu_pct', 'load_1m', 'memory_total_bytes', 'memory_used_bytes', 'memory_available_bytes', 'memory_pct', 'swap_used_bytes', 'cpu_psi_some_avg10', 'cpu_psi_some_avg60', 'cpu_psi_some_avg300', 'cpu_psi_some_total_us', 'memory_psi_some_avg10', 'memory_psi_some_avg60', 'memory_psi_some_avg300', 'memory_psi_some_total_us', 'io_psi_some_avg10', 'io_psi_some_avg60', 'io_psi_some_avg300', 'io_psi_some_total_us', 'disk_read_bytes_total', 'disk_write_bytes_total', 'cpu_first_interval_warmup']

def projection(o):

 p,m,d=o["psi"],o["memory"],o["disk_io"]

 return {"ts_utc":o["ts_utc"],"monotonic_ns":str(o["monotonic_ns"]),

 "cpu_pct":format(o["cpu_pct"],".12g"),"load_1m":format(o["load_average"][0],".12g"),

 "memory_total_bytes":str(m["total_bytes"]),"memory_used_bytes":str(m["used_bytes"]),

 "memory_available_bytes":str(m["available_bytes"]),"memory_pct":format(m["percent"],".12g"),

 "swap_used_bytes":str(o["swap"]["used_bytes"]),

 "cpu_psi_some_avg10":format(p["cpu"]["some"]["avg10"],".12g"),

 "cpu_psi_some_avg60":format(p["cpu"]["some"]["avg60"],".12g"),

 "cpu_psi_some_avg300":format(p["cpu"]["some"]["avg300"],".12g"),

 "cpu_psi_some_total_us":str(p["cpu"]["some"]["total"]),

 "memory_psi_some_avg10":format(p["memory"]["some"]["avg10"],".12g"),

 "memory_psi_some_avg60":format(p["memory"]["some"]["avg60"],".12g"),

 "memory_psi_some_avg300":format(p["memory"]["some"]["avg300"],".12g"),

 "memory_psi_some_total_us":str(p["memory"]["some"]["total"]),

 "io_psi_some_avg10":format(p["io"]["some"]["avg10"],".12g"),

 "io_psi_some_avg60":format(p["io"]["some"]["avg60"],".12g"),

 "io_psi_some_avg300":format(p["io"]["some"]["avg300"],".12g"),

 "io_psi_some_total_us":str(p["io"]["some"]["total"]),

 "disk_read_bytes_total":str(d["read_bytes"]),"disk_write_bytes_total":str(d["write_bytes"]),

 "cpu_first_interval_warmup":str(bool(o["quality"]["cpu_first_interval_warmup"])).lower()}

def main():

 ap=argparse.ArgumentParser(); ap.add_argument("--capture-dir",required=True); cap=Path(ap.parse_args().capture_dir).resolve()

 root=cap.parents[2]; hosts=[]; proc=0; total=0; runids=set(); counts=Counter()

 with (cap/"telemetry.jsonl").open(encoding="utf-8") as f:

  for n,line in enumerate(f,1):

   o=json.loads(line); total+=1; runids.add(o.get("run_id"))

   if o.get("record_type")=="host_sample": hosts.append(o)

   elif o.get("record_type")=="process_sample": proc+=1; counts[o.get("ts_utc")]+=1

   else: raise ValueError(f"Unknown record type at line {n}")

 with (cap/"host_samples.csv").open(encoding="utf-8-sig",newline="") as f:

  reader=csv.DictReader(f); rows=list(reader)

  if reader.fieldnames!=FIELDS: raise ValueError("Unexpected CSV header")

 if len(rows)!=len(hosts): raise ValueError("CSV row count differs from JSONL host count")

 for i,(row,obj) in enumerate(zip(rows,hosts),1):

  for key,val in projection(obj).items():

   actual=row.get(key)

   if key in ("cpu_pct","load_1m","memory_pct") or "_avg" in key:

    if actual is None or abs(float(actual)-float(val))>1e-10: raise ValueError(f"CSV mismatch row {i}: {key}")

   elif actual!=val: raise ValueError(f"CSV mismatch row {i}: {key}")

 manifest=json.loads((cap/"capture_manifest.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8")); checks=[]

 for name,item in manifest["artifacts"].items():

  data=(root/item["relative_path"]).read_bytes()

  ok=len(data)==item["size_bytes"] and hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest()==item["sha256"]

  checks.append(ok)

  if not ok: raise ValueError(f"Artifact integrity mismatch: {name}")

 if len(counts)!=len(hosts) or set(counts.values())!={316}: raise ValueError("Unexpected process coverage")

 print(f"PASS JSONL syntax and counts: {total:,} records = {len(hosts)} host + {proc:,} process")

 print(f"PASS process coverage: 316 rows at each of {len(counts)} timestamps")

 print(f"PASS CSV projection: {len(rows)} rows x {len(FIELDS)} fields; exact match including monotonic_ns")

 print(f"PASS artifact integrity: {sum(checks)}/{len(checks)} listed size/SHA-256 pairs match")

 print(f"Run ID: {sorted(runids)}")

 print(f"Target caveat: captured {manifest['target_fit']['captured_guest']}; project target {manifest['target_fit']['specified_project_target']}")

if __name__=="__main__": main()

Engineering review and evidence scope

AIOS Package Quality Review

Reviewed 15 November 2026.

Improvements made

The composite component overview now includes the decision writer's SQLite status and recommendation projection write, matching the container architecture. The dashboard response filter returns its safe payload to the HTTP routes before the viewer receives it. Validated inference results return through the request handler. Peer, request, and target rejection outcomes have explicit paths to the audit writer.

The general explanatory note is now a diagram-wide legend. Acronyms in the legend are expanded. The SVG, PNG, and JPG exports were regenerated from the updated PlantUML source and the new PNG was visually inspected. The notation review's view count and damaged quotation text were corrected. These edits describe proposed behavior, not an implemented or tested service.

Checks completed

CheckObserved resultLimit
Requirements identifiers52 rows, 52 unique IDsRequirement quality still needs team approval
Verification coverageEvery requirement has a verification methodMethods are planned checks, not execution results
Word package structure20 DOCX archives and main document XML parts opened successfully, including references and a QA copyThis does not establish page-layout quality; a fresh render of all Word/PDF pages was not completed
Markdown navigationRelative Markdown links resolved within the packageExternal websites were not exhaustively link-checked
Recorded telemetryExisting validator passed 19,337 records: 61 host and 19,276 process rows; CSV matched 61 by 24 fields; all five capture hashes matchedThis is a retained passive Ubuntu 26.04.1 capture
Composite overviewDirected dashed relationships, six distinct service boundaries, filtered read-only viewer path, projection persistence, guarded action and rejection audit pathsDetailed service diagrams present selected relationships; the companion guide explains the added cross-service paths

The overview is intentionally identified as a composite. A standard C4 component diagram scopes one container; the six scoped views provide those decompositions. C4 permits different notation when types, responsibilities, relationships, and legends are clear. See [component scope](https://c4model.com/diagrams/component) and [notation guidance](https://c4model.com/diagrams/notation).

Evidence still required for project acceptance

The package's closure register already records the outstanding work: Ubuntu 24.04 target validation, an integrated prototype with safety acceptance results, measured benefit and overhead under representative workloads, local needs evidence where required, and team or supervisor decisions on contracts and thresholds. Those outcomes cannot be supplied by documentation edits. The saved capture does not establish CPU-control safety, model accuracy, forecasting benefit, or collector overhead in isolation.

Using the package

At the time of the 15 November review, use the whole-system SVG for zooming into the full map and the six scoped views for close reading; the Word guide then covered only the scoped views. The 16 November update below supersedes that guide description and records the refreshed eight-page suite containing both the composite map and all six scoped views. No claim of perfect implementation or a guaranteed grade is made by this review.

Update — 16 November 2026

The C4 component notation and dependent deliverables have since been refreshed and rechecked. All seven component views now use UML1 component glyphs with two compact adjacent tabs at the upper-left of every component: 60 components in total. The shared verifier passed for component counts, tab coordinates, UML1 style, and byte-identical source/render SVG, PNG, and JPG files. The contact sheet and standalone C4.zip were refreshed, and the archive no longer includes the stray node_probe.tmp render artifact.

The component architecture guide was rebuilt as an eight-page landscape DOCX and exported to PDF. All eight PDF pages were rendered and visually reviewed; the guide contains the whole-system map and six service-scoped views, with no blank pages or clipped figures. The consolidated HTML handbook was regenerated and its browser QA passed with 16 chapters, 36 figures, no broken images or anchors, no overflow at desktop or mobile width, no external resource dependencies, and no JavaScript errors.

The canonical version 4 university-template presentation has 37 slides: 25 visible talk slides and 12 hidden technical backup slides. Version 4 corrects the full authenticated-action sequence picture to use the exact canonical image and preserve its aspect ratio. All 11 C4 render PNGs and four sequence PNGs match their project sources byte-for-byte. Artifact Tool imported and rendered all 37 slides; package integrity and slide-layout checks report zero findings. The contact sheet was regenerated and reviewed; slides 10 and 26–28 were inspected individually. Native PowerPoint and font rendering are unverified. These checks do not establish target-host operation or safety acceptance.

The SPMP was revised into a whole-project management baseline for the monitor → process → predict → decide → bounded act product. It records a 133–195 person-day preliminary base estimate with contingency explicitly unquantified, a 16-sprint course-aligned forecast, Scrum estimation and events, capacity assumptions, risk scoring, course-rubric mapping, and separate safety gates for CPU, memory, and I/O actions. Its current twelve-page Word/PDF rendering was inspected. The canonical plan is 06_Project_Management/AIOS_Software_Project_Management_Plan.docx with the matching PDF beside it. Scrum role assignments, task status, team availability, and course dates other than the supplied 19 November 2026 GP1 midterm still require team/supervisor confirmation.

The curated release lists 420 source files and includes the manifest as the 421st ZIP entry. The verifier checked every listed path, size, and SHA-256 against the workspace, matched archive contents to source files, and passed ZIP CRC. It also checked 135 directed relationships across all 11 C4 sources and their dashed SVG renders.

Source: 10_Evidence_Closure/Package_Quality_Review.md

Architecture update — 18 November 2026

The current C4 baseline is now the functional control-loop architecture in 11_C4_Architecture/AIOS_Functional_C4_Architecture.md. Its Level 1 context, Level 2 container, and Level 3 Real-Time Optimizer Daemon component views are the numbered 15–17 assets. The former five-layer and service-oriented C4 views are superseded for this runtime design. The current component view shows functional modules, paired UML1 tabs, required/provided ports, and labeled dashed one-way connections for inference, safety, rollback, kernel actuation, audit, and feedback.

The design separates the runtime sampler from the inference worker, offline model training, persistence, and operations exporter. PSI and cgroup v2 controls are cited to Linux kernel documentation; candidate writes remain allowlisted and fail closed when checks or rollback journaling fail. The architecture is a proposal and has not been validated against a deployed target kernel or measured workload.

The functional C4 images are embedded in this chapter, editable PlantUML and image files are under 11_C4_Architecture/sources/, and the complete current file digest list is in PACKAGE_MANIFEST.csv. The C4 release bundle and project ZIP were refreshed. The new diagrams were visually reviewed; their PlantUML sources were not compiled in this update.

15 Glossary and engineering decisions

These definitions keep the presentation and implementation discussion consistent.

TermMeaning
AIOSAI-Native Adaptive Operating System; proposed Ubuntu user-space services
C4 containerRunnable application or data store, not necessarily a Docker container
ComponentLogical responsibility inside a service container
PSIPressure Stall Information; a current Linux pressure signal
cgroups v2Linux control-group hierarchy and resource interfaces
cpu.weightRelative CPU scheduling weight under contention; not a reservation
CPU affinitySet of logical CPUs on which a task or service may run
CPU quotaUpper CPU-time allowance over a period
SO_PEERCREDKernel-reported credentials of a Unix-domain-socket peer
PID plus start timeProcess-instance reference used to detect PID reuse
DTOData Transfer Object used for a limited dashboard view
RSSResident Set Size; memory resident in physical RAM
WALWrite-Ahead Log used by SQLite in the corresponding mode
STRIDESpoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, elevation of privilege
OBSERVE_ONLYObservation and reporting mode without AIOS resource writes
LEAVEDecision to perform no resource adjustment
TBDDesign choice or contract still to be agreed
